question: In the context of this course, what does the term 'data' refer to?
options: All types of information, down to the most basic numbers and strings
Only numeric values such as integers and floats, never strings or text
Only information that has been saved permanently to a file or a database
Only the values a program prints to the screen, such as "Hello World!"
correctAnswer: All types of information, down to the most basic numbers and strings
explanation: Data is a broad term covering all types of information. Even the string "Hello World!" is data, and even complex data usually breaks down into numbers and strings.

question: Fill in the blank: Data structures refer to how data is _____.
explanation: A data structure is about how data is organized.

question: In the boots and shoes example, what did reordering the footwear (two shoes first, then two boots) give us?
options: A faster way to compile the inventory program
Lower memory usage for every item in the inventory
Automatic sorting of the footwear by size
explanation: Reorganizing the inventory so the shoes came first and boots after made the items easier to identify.

question: In the footwear example, what problem does assigning each item an index solve?
options: It lets two shoes share one identifier without conflicts
It reduces how much memory the collection of footwear needs to use
It sorts the footwear so boots and shoes always alternate in order
It removes ambiguity, e.g. 'the second shoe' from the left or the right
correctAnswer: It removes ambiguity, e.g. 'the second shoe' from the left or the right
explanation: With an identifier you can ask for 'the shoe at index 2' and get exactly what you wanted instead of wondering which direction to count from.

question: A program stores three strings in three separate variables, then the same program is rewritten to store them in one array. What changed?
options: Only the organization of the data changed
The data changed, because arrays store copies of each string
The output changed, because arrays join the strings differently
The program now stores all three strings on the heap instead
correctAnswer: Only the organization of the data changed
explanation: Both versions output the same message. The only difference is that three independent string variables were reorganized into a collection (array) of three strings.

question: Short answer: Why does the choice of data structure matter beyond keeping things tidy?
options: It mostly affects readability, since modern compilers optimize away any speed differences
It can change how fast code runs by orders of magnitude, and whether software can handle the load at all
It only matters for programs that store strings, since numbers are handled the same way
It determines which compiler and operating system the program needs to run
correctAnswer: It can change how fast code runs by orders of magnitude, and whether software can handle the load at all
explanation: Data organization can make a program faster or slower by orders of magnitude. For large data or apps used by thousands of people, it can decide whether the software runs or conks out under load.

question: Fill in the blank: A data type is a specification on the use of a particular set of _____.
explanation: A data type specifies how a particular set of bits/bytes is used.

question: Which are the small building blocks data types are built from?
explanation: Data types are built from small building blocks: integers, floats, and chars.

question: Choosing short vs. long int, or float vs. double, is an example of which trade-off?
explanation: Larger types use more space but hold larger values or more precision, so it is a trade-off between space and accuracy.

question: According to the slides, what are functions/methods such as GetSum() and ToString() in relation to data types?
options: Memory regions where the data is stored while the program runs
Primary data types that the compiler provides by default
Pointer types used to reach data stored on the heap
explanation: Functions/methods are the operations performed on the data.

question: Complete the definition: A data type is a set of values and _____.
options: a fixed size in bytes that every compiler must use
a memory address where those values are stored at runtime
a collection of operations on those values
a pointer to the next value in the sequence
correctAnswer: a collection of operations on those values
explanation: A data type is a set of values and a collection of operations on those values. Defining your own data types is often an effective way to organize software.

question: Which of these is a PRIMARY data type in C?
explanation: Primary C data types are Integers, Characters, Float, Double and Void.

question: Which of these is a SECONDARY data type in C?
explanation: Secondary C data types are Array, Pointer, Structure, Union and Enum.

question: Which list contains ONLY primary C data types?
explanation: The five primary types are Integers, Characters, Float, Double and Void.

question: According to the ISO C definition, what is the MINIMUM size of an int?
explanation: ISO C sets the minimum size of an int at 2 bytes, although on most modern 64-bit systems an int is actually 4 bytes.

question: On most modern 64-bit systems, how large is an int?
explanation: The minimum is 2 bytes, but most modern 64-bit systems use a 4-byte int.

question: What does ISO C say about the size of a long?
options: Its minimum is 4 bytes, and on modern 64-bit systems it can be 4 or 8 bytes depending on the platform
Its minimum is 8 bytes, and on modern 64-bit systems it is always exactly 8 bytes on every platform
It is always the same size as an int, so it is 2 bytes minimum and 4 bytes on modern systems
Its minimum is 2 bytes, and on modern 64-bit systems it is fixed at 4 bytes by the ISO C standard
correctAnswer: Its minimum is 4 bytes, and on modern 64-bit systems it can be 4 or 8 bytes depending on the platform
explanation: A long has a minimum of 4 bytes; on modern 64-bit systems it is platform dependent (4 or 8 bytes).

question: Which data type is declared to be 8 bytes in length?
explanation: A long long is declared to be 8 bytes.

question: Which header gives you integer types with a guaranteed size, such as int32_t?
explanation: Including <stdint.h> gives int16_t, int32_t and int64_t, which have guaranteed lengths.

question: How many bytes is an int16_t guaranteed to be?
explanation: int16_t is guaranteed to be 16 bits, which is 2 bytes.

question: Match the type to its guaranteed size: int64_t is _____.
explanation: int16_t = 2 bytes, int32_t = 4 bytes, int64_t = 8 bytes.

question: What does ISO C mandate as the fixed size of a long double?
options: 8 bytes, the same as a double on every platform
Nothing; there is no mandated fixed size
10 bytes, matching the x87 extended precision format
16 bytes, with 10 bytes used and 6 bytes of padding
correctAnswer: Nothing; there is no mandated fixed size
explanation: There is no mandated size for long double. It depends entirely on the hardware architecture, OS and compiler.

question: Using gcc on an x86/x64 platform (Linux or macOS), how big is a long double and how much of it holds the value?
options: 10 bytes, all used, with no padding added by gcc
16 bytes, all of which are used to hold the value
16 bytes, but only 10 bytes hold the value and 6 are padding
8 bytes, the same as a double, with no padding
correctAnswer: 16 bytes, but only 10 bytes hold the value and 6 are padding
explanation: With gcc on x86/x64, a long double is 16 bytes, of which only 10 hold the value and 6 are padded.

question: Using the Microsoft Visual C compiler on Windows (x86/x64), how big is a long double?
options: 4 bytes, the same as a float
8 bytes, the same as a double
correctAnswer: 8 bytes, the same as a double
explanation: With MSVC, a long double is 8 bytes, which is the same as a double. That is why dataTypeSize.c says there's no use printing a long double on Windows.

question: What is an enum used for?
options: To define a data type that holds constants (unchangeable values)
To dynamically allocate memory for a group of related values
To store the address of another variable
To group variables of different types into one record
correctAnswer: To define a data type that holds constants (unchangeable values)
explanation: An enum defines a data type to hold/contain constants.

question: Given: enum MyLevels { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH }; What is the value of HIGH?
explanation: With default values, enum constants start at 0, so LOW = 0, MEDIUM = 1, HIGH = 2.

question: Given: enum MyLevels { LOW = 25, MEDIUM = 50, HIGH = 75 }; What is the value of MEDIUM?
explanation: You can set your own enum values. Here MEDIUM is explicitly set to 50.

question: Fill in the blank: A pointer is a variable that stores the _____ of another variable.
explanation: A pointer stores the address of a memory location of another variable.

question: Short answer: What is the key to understanding pointers?
options: Understanding how memory is organized and managed in a C program
Memorizing the exact size in bytes of every data type on every platform
Knowing how printf formats addresses with the %p and %X specifiers
Understanding how enums assign integer values to named constants
correctAnswer: Understanding how memory is organized and managed in a C program
explanation: Pointers contain addresses in memory, so without understanding how memory is organized and managed, it is hard to understand how pointers work.

question: Which statement about pointers is TRUE?
options: A pointer stores both the address and the type of the data it points to
Nothing inherent in a pointer indicates what type of data it references; it only contains an address
A pointer can only point to integers, since memory addresses themselves are just integers
A pointer always points to memory on the heap, because stack variables have no fixed address
correctAnswer: Nothing inherent in a pointer indicates what type of data it references; it only contains an address
explanation: A pointer is normally declared with a type (e.g. pointer to char), but the pointer itself only contains an address.

question: Which three types of memory does a compiled C program work with?
explanation: A C program works with static/global memory, the stack, and the heap.

question: Which memory region holds global and statically declared variables that exist from program start until it terminates?
explanation: Static and global variables are allocated when the program starts and remain until it terminates.

question: What is the difference in scope between global variables and static variables?
options: All functions can access global variables, but a static variable's scope is restricted to its defining function
There is no difference; both kinds can be accessed from every function in the program
Static variables are accessible from every function, but global variables only from main
Global variables live on the heap and static variables live on the stack
correctAnswer: All functions can access global variables, but a static variable's scope is restricted to its defining function
explanation: Both use static memory, but the scope of static variables is restricted to their defining function.

question: Which memory region is sometimes called 'automatic memory'?
explanation: The stack is sometimes called automatic memory. Variables declared in a function, or passed into one, live there only while the function is executing.

question: A variable declared inside a function lives in which memory region, and for how long?
options: Static memory, until the program ends
Heap, until it is released with free()
Stack, only while the function is executing
correctAnswer: Stack, only while the function is executing
explanation: Stack variables are restricted to their function in scope, and their lifetime is limited to the time the function is executing.

question: Memory you allocate dynamically comes from which region, and how long does it exist?
explanation: Dynamic memory comes from the heap, is referenced by a pointer, and exists until it is released.

question: Which operator returns the memory address of a variable?
explanation: The & (address-of) operator gives the physical memory address of a variable.

question: Variable x is stored at memory address 2712. What does &x evaluate to?
explanation: &x gives the address of x, which is 2712 in this example. The programmer sees 'x'; the operating system sees address 2712. The real address depends on the machine and execution time.

question: What is the '*' operator called when used on a pointer?
options: Member access operator, used to reach fields of a struct
Address-of operator, which returns where a variable is stored
Multiplication operator, applied to the pointer's address
explanation: If the address of a variable is known, '*' gives the contents at that address.
p holds the address of x, so *p = 40 writes 40 into x.

question: Which header must you include to use malloc()?
explanation: malloc() is declared in <stdlib.h>: void* malloc(size_t numBytes);

question: What does malloc() return if the system runs out of memory on the heap?
explanation: If the heap runs out of memory, malloc() returns NULL, so you should always check its result.

question: malloc() returns a void*. What is the programmer's responsibility?
options: Nothing; C converts it automatically into the right struct
Cast the pointer to the type (shape) of pointer you want
correctAnswer: Cast the pointer to the type (shape) of pointer you want
explanation: It is your responsibility to cast the void* to the pointer type you need, e.g. (MyDate*)malloc(sizeof(MyDate)).

question: How long does memory allocated with malloc() exist?
options: Until the next call to malloc()
explanation: Dynamically allocated memory persists for as long as you want it to, until you free it.

question: Short answer: Why use a structure to store a date instead of separate month, day and year variables?
options: A structure groups logically related variables together so you don't have to track three separate variables for every date
Structures use less memory than separate int variables, because the compiler packs all of the members tightly together
Separate variables are not allowed in C when the values belong together, so a structure is required
Structures print faster with printf, since all the members are output in a single call
correctAnswer: A structure groups logically related variables together so you don't have to track three separate variables for every date
explanation: With separate variables you'd need month/day/year and purchaseMonth/purchaseDay/purchaseYear, and so on. A structure groups those logically related values together.

options: Reserves memory for three integers named month, day and year
Defines a new type, struct date, but reserves no storage
Declares a variable called date that holds three integers
Allocates a date on the heap that must later be freed
correctAnswer: Defines a new type, struct date, but reserves no storage
explanation: Defining a structure only tells the compiler what it looks like. Declaring a variable of that type is what reserves memory.

question: Which line actually causes memory to be reserved?
options: struct date { int month; int day; int year; };
explanation: Declaring the variable today of type struct date reserves storage for its three integer members.

question: Which is a valid way to declare two struct date variables on the same line?
explanation: You can declare variables separately or include both declarations on one line: struct date today, purchaseDate;

question: Fill in the blank: To set the day of the struct variable today to 25, you write _____.
explanation: A structure member is accessed with the variable name, a period, then the member name.

question: Which statement correctly tests whether the month in today is December?
explanation: Use the dot operator to reach the member and == to compare. A single = would assign instead of compare.

question: today.year is the int 2015. What is the value of today.year / 100?
explanation: Structure members follow the same expression rules as ordinary variables, so int / int is integer division: 2015 / 100 = 20.

question: The 'tomorrow's date' program was required to properly handle which two special cases?
options: February 29 in a leap year, and a date mistakenly entered as December 32nd
Leap years, and dates entered in the wrong YYYY-MM-DD format
A date at the end of a week, and a date at the end of a quarter
A date at the end of a month, and a date at the end of a year (December 31)
correctAnswer: A date at the end of a month, and a date at the end of a year (December 31)
explanation: The problem required handling end-of-month and end-of-year (December 31). Leap year logic was noted in date.c as a further enhancement but not implemented.

question: In date.c, the user enters 2025-12-31. What does tomorrow get set to?
explanation: It's the last day of the month and the month is 12, so day = 1, month = 1, year = year + 1, with the note 'Happy New Year!!'.

question: In date.c, the user enters 2025-04-30. Which branch runs?
options: None; the program crashes on April 31
explanation: April has 30 days, so day == numberOfDaysInEachMonth[3] and month isn't 12. Tomorrow becomes 2025-05-01.

question: In date.c, why is the array indexed as numberOfDaysInEachMonth[today.month - 1]?
options: Because February must be skipped when it is not a leap year
Because months are stored in reverse order inside the array
Because arrays start at index 0 but months are numbered 1 to 12
Because index 12 would trigger a compiler warning
correctAnswer: Because arrays start at index 0 but months are numbered 1 to 12
explanation: January (month 1) is at index 0, so you subtract 1 from the month number.

question: What is a known limitation of date.c as written?
options: It can't handle the end of a month, so day 31 becomes day 32
It can't handle December 31, so the year never increments
It never frees the memory it allocates with malloc() for randomDay
It doesn't handle leap years; February always has 28 days
correctAnswer: It doesn't handle leap years; February always has 28 days
explanation: The array hard-codes 28 days for February. The comments note leap year logic and input validation as things to add.

question: In date.c, randomDay is declared as MyDate* and today as MyDate. Why does the code use randomDay->year but today.year?
options: -> is used for members accessed through a pointer; . is used on a struct variable directly
-> is faster than . because it skips copying the struct, so it is used for larger structs
-> is only for heap memory and . is only for stack memory
It is a typo; both should use . since randomDay and today are both MyDate structs
correctAnswer: -> is used for members accessed through a pointer; . is used on a struct variable directly
explanation: randomDay is a pointer to a MyDate (allocated with malloc), so its members are accessed with ->. today is an actual struct variable, so it uses the dot operator. randomDay->year is equivalent to (*randomDay).year.

question: Which line correctly allocates a MyDate struct on the heap, as in date.c?
explanation: Request sizeof(MyDate) bytes, then cast the returned void* to MyDate*.

question: What is the last thing date.c must do with randomDay before returning?
options: Nothing; heap memory is freed automatically when main returns
explanation: The code ends with free(randomDay) because memory from malloc must be freed when no longer needed.

question: In date.c: char* inpPtr = inpDateStr; This line is equivalent to which of the following?
explanation: Using an array's name without an index gives the address of the base (first element) of the array.

question: The user typed "2025-10-29" into inpDateStr. After char* inpPtr = inpDateStr; inpPtr += 4; what is *inpPtr?
explanation: Indexes 0-3 are the year, so moving 4 characters ahead lands on index 4, the first '-'.

question: Continuing: after another inpPtr += 4; (so 8 characters from the start of "2025-10-29"), what is *inpPtr?
explanation: In YYYY-MM-DD, index 8 is the first D character. For "2025-10-29" that's '2'.

question: In date.c, which pair of functions reads a line of input and then parses YYYY-MM-DD out of it?
explanation: fgets reads the line into inpDateStr, then sscanf(inpDateStr, "%d-%d-%d", &today.year, &today.month, &today.day) parses it.

question: In dataTypeSize.c, an unsigned char initialized to 0 is decremented by 1. What value is printed?
explanation: An unsigned char can't be negative, so it wraps around to its maximum value, 255.

question: In dataTypeSize.c, an unsigned short initialized to 0 is decremented by 1. What value is printed?
explanation: A 2-byte unsigned short wraps around to its maximum, 65535.

question: In dataTypeSize.c, signed char signChar = 127; signChar++; What is printed on a typical system?
explanation: 127 is the maximum of a signed char, so incrementing overflows and wraps to the minimum, -128.

question: In dataTypeSize.c, signed short signShort = 32767; signShort++; What is printed on a typical system?
explanation: 32767 is the max signed short, so incrementing wraps to the minimum, -32768.

question: What does sizeof(char) return?
options: It depends on the string length
explanation: A char is always 1 byte.

question: According to dataTypeSize.c, how many decimal places of accuracy does a float have vs. a double?
explanation: The program prints a float to 6 decimal places and a double to 15 decimal places.

question: Which of the following reference books is listed for this course?
options: Clean Code by Robert C. Martin
A Common-Sense Guide to Data Structures and Algorithms by Jay Wengrow
The Pragmatic Programmer by David Thomas and Andrew Hunt
Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software
correctAnswer: A Common-Sense Guide to Data Structures and Algorithms by Jay Wengrow
explanation: References include Wengrow's Common-Sense Guide, Kochan's Programming in C, Lafore's Data Structures and Algorithms in Java, Subero's Codeless Data Structures and Algorithms, and Kamthane's Introduction to Data Structures in C.
